newsitem.title: USA: Insured losses from Fran seen large but manageable.
newsitem.headline: Insured losses from Fran seen large but manageable.

text.p: U.S. insurers face large losses from Hurricane Fran, but the losses are not likely to be serious enough to threaten them with insolvency or allow them to boost the rates they charge customers.

But the damage from Hurricane Fran was expected to be serious enough to hit global reinsurers with some losses as well, said Sean Mooney, economist and senior vice president at Insurance Information Institute.
The storm, which slammed into the Carolina coast Thursday night, was being compared in the insurance industry to Hurricanes Opal and Hugo.

Opal caused insured damage of about $2.1 billion in 1995. Hugo, which resulted in overall insured damage of $4.2 billion in 1989, caused about $2.5 billion in insured damage in the United States, Mooney said.
"With that kind of a storm, it would trigger reinsurance coverage for many of the companies so that this would be a loss for European, Asian...the world reinsurance market," Mooney said.

Even so, U.S. insurers have come to expect storms like Hurricane Fran, Mooney said. And they have begun to budget a bit more for hurricanes these days because of their increasing frequency and severity, he said.
"A storm like this you expect once every two or three years," he said. "So this is kind of a normal pattern."
"In general, companies would not be happy to take the loss, but would absorb it as the normal range of storms that they expect," Mooney said.
The largest personal property insurer in North Carolina is Nationwide Insurance, with 18.24 percent of the market.

State Farm ranks second with 16.5 percent of the market in North Carolina, followed by Integon with 12.14 percent and Allstate Corp with 10.01 percent, according to the Insurance Information Institute.
In South Carolina, State Farm is the leading personal property insurer with 31.85 percent of the market followed by Allstate with 14.22 percent and Nationwide with 8.52 percent.
U.S. property-casualty insurers are likely to show some losses in the third quarter.
But, said Conning & Co analyst Jeff Thompson, "I don't think it's going to be all that significant."
State Farm has already said initial indications are that property damage claims from Fran will not rival Hugo.
Because the losses are likely to be within the range U.S. insurers expect in a normal year, availability and pricing of insurance is not likely to change much, Mooney said.
Homeowners insurance will still be difficult to obtain in some areas, but the pricing already reflects expectations of storms of this magnitude, he said.
Losses would have to exceed about $10 billion before the availability and pricing of reinsurance and property insurance might be affected substantially, he said.
And a loss of about $50 billion would be needed to harden rates for commercial lines of insurance, he said.
However, even though losses from Fran were likely to come in as budgeted, overall catastrophic losses this year are beginning to be sizable.
The first half of 1996 was the second costliest in the past 14 years.

In the first quarter, blizzards and bitter cold resulted in insured losses of $2.55 billion. Severe thunderstorms, tornadoes and hail caused another $1.65 billion in insured losses in the second quarter.
Hurricane Bertha, which struck the eastern United States in early July, cased an estimated $135 million in insured property damage.
And more losses are still possible as the hurricane season runs through November.
"This has been a pretty tough year," Thompson said.
